I am 62 years old and I have farmed in Quzhou County for more than forty years. I finished middle school, so I can read the numbers on fertilizer bags and understand what the extension people tell me, but I still trust my own eyes and what my neighbors do more than any book. I have about ten mu of good irrigated land, and it is just me and my wife working it now — my son is in Shijiazhuang working construction.

My winter wheat went in last October. I rotary-tilled the soil before sowing and put down about thirty jin of improved wheat seed per mu. Now it is early spring and the wheat is greening up. I will irrigate it three times in total this cycle: the winter irrigation is already done, and I will do two more — one at jointing and one at heading if the dry wind keeps up. For fertilizer, I broadcast about one hundred jin of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and I will topdress another thirty jin of urea per mu when the wheat starts jointing. The extension agent keeps saying I should cut back on nitrogen, but two years ago I tried using less and my yield dropped by nearly a hundred jin per mu, so I went back to my usual amount. I expect about one thousand jin per mu if we do not get a late frost. I will spray pesticides four times: herbicide once, and insecticide two or three times if I see aphids.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize on the same eight mu. There is no time to waste — if you wait more than three or four days, the maize will not mature before the cold comes. I buy hybrid seed every year, Denghai or Nongda, about one package per mu. I do not till for maize; I plant straight into the wheat stubble to save time. I put down compound fertilizer with the planter, about eighty to one hundred jin per mu. Maize is easier than wheat — two irrigations if it does not rain, and three pesticide sprays. I expect about eleven hundred jin per mu.

I still keep two mu of cotton because the price was decent last year, though at my age the work is getting hard. Cotton needs constant attention — pruning, and spraying for insects almost every week in July and August. I rotary-till that plot in spring and plant guoxinmian in April. I use about one hundred jin of compound fertilizer per mu. The cotton needs two irrigations and I will spray pesticides about twelve times. I am telling my wife this might be the last year for cotton — my back is not what it used to be, and hired labor is too expensive.

Wheat and maize are my bread and butter. They are stable, I have the tractor for them, and I know them like the back of my hand. Cotton is my gamble for extra cash, but the labor is wearing me down.
